name: โรคระบบประสาทเบาหวาน
preview_text: อาการชาและแสบร้อนของเส้นประสาทส่วนปลายที่เป็นเบาหวานไม่ใช่โรคเดียว แต่มีรูปแบบที่แตกต่างกันถึง 4 รูปแบบ และผู้ป่วยส่วนใหญ่สังเกตเห็นว่าความรู้สึกและความเจ็บปวดดีขึ้นภายใน 6-12 สัปดาห์หลังการฝังเข็ม
categories: ["อาการปวดเส้นประสาทและโรคระบบประสาท", "โรคเบาหวาน", "ภาวะสมองและระบบประสาท"]
synonyms: ["Diabetes-induced Peripheral Neuropathy", "Diabetes-related Nerve Damage", "Neuropathy Due To Diabetes", "Diabetic peripheral neuropathy"]
conventional_description: Diabetic neuropathy is nerve damage caused by chronically high blood sugar levels. It typically begins in the feet and legs, then may progress to the hands, causing numbness, tingling, burning pain, and muscle weakness. The diagnosis is usually made based on symptoms and a physical exam, sometimes confirmed with nerve conduction studies.
conventional_treatments: Standard treatment focuses on tight blood sugar control to slow progression, along with medications to manage pain. Commonly prescribed drugs include gabapentin, pregabalin, duloxetine, and tricyclic antidepressants. Topical capsaicin cream may also be used. Despite these options, many patients find only partial relief and struggle with side effects like drowsiness or dizziness.
tcm_understanding:
In TCM, diabetic neuropathy (消渴病痹症) is understood as a complication of Xiao Ke, the pattern of wasting and thirst that underlies diabetes. Years of high blood sugar deplete the body's Qi and Yin - the vital energy and cooling fluids that nourish every tissue. Without sufficient Qi and Yin, the nerves become undernourished and vulnerable to further damage from stagnation, cold, or phlegm.
The specific symptoms a person experiences reveal which pattern is dominant. If Qi is too weak to move blood, stagnation sets in, and the result is sharp, stabbing pain that worsens at night. If Yin is drained, empty heat rises, causing burning sensations, night sweats, and a dry mouth.
When the body's warming Yang is also depleted, cold can invade the channels, leading to severe, cold pain that improves with warmth. And if the Spleen's ability to transform fluids is impaired, phlegm-dampness accumulates, producing a heavy, cotton-walking numbness.
Because the root is always some form of deficiency, TCM treatment never simply numbs the pain. Instead, it aims to rebuild Qi and Yin while clearing the specific obstruction - whether that means moving blood, warming the channels, or drying phlegm. This is why two people with identical Western diagnoses may receive entirely different acupuncture point combinations and herbal formulas.
classical_quote: 「消渴之人，必数食甘美而多肥也，肥者令人内热，甘者令人中满，故其气上溢，转为消渴。久则经络涩滞，荣卫不行，四肢不得禀水谷气，故痿痹不仁。」
classical_translation: "Those with Xiao Ke invariably eat rich and sweet foods frequently; fatty foods generate internal Heat, and sweet foods cause fullness in the center, so the Qi overflows and turns into Xiao Ke. Over time, the channels and collaterals become obstructed, the nutritive and defensive Qi fail to circulate, and the four limbs do not receive the essence of food and water, leading to atrophy, numbness, and bi syndrome."
classical_source:
Zhu Bing Yuan Hou Lun (Treatise on the Origins and Symptoms of Diseases)  ,  Chapter on Xiao Ke (Wasting and Thirsting) 									·
More references
tcm_diagnosis:
If the person feels numbness and tingling with a dull ache that turns into sharp stabbing pain at night, and they also complain of being easily tired, short of breath, and prone to spontaneous sweating, the practitioner suspects Qi deficiency failing to move blood. The tongue is often pale with a darkish hue and small stasis spots, while the pulse feels thin and hesitant.
When the pain has a burning quality, worse at night, and the limbs feel sore or hot, the picture shifts toward Yin deficiency. These individuals often have a dry mouth, a sensation of heat in the palms and soles, and constipation. The tongue appears red or dark red with little coating, and the pulse is thin and rapid or hesitant.
If the limbs are distinctly cold to the touch, the pain is severe and cramping, and warmth brings relief while cold weather makes it worse, cold congealing the channels is the key pattern. There is often an overall aversion to cold. The tongue is pale or dark with a white slippery coating, and the pulse is deep, thin, and hesitant.
When numbness feels heavy, as if walking on cotton, and the person is overweight with a sticky taste in the mouth, chest tightness, and a thick greasy tongue coating, phlegm-dampness obstructing the collaterals is likely. The tongue is swollen with teeth marks and a thick white coating, and the pulse is slippery or hesitant.

patterns.symptoms: ["Fixed stabbing pain that worsens at rest", "Numbness and tingling in the limbs", "Severe fatigue and shortness of breath", "Dull or dusky facial complexion", "Spontaneous sweating with mild activity"]
patterns.worse_with: Overexertion and exhaustion, Stress and emotional upset, Cold exposure, Greasy, fried, or sugary foods, Prolonged inactivity
patterns.better_with: Rest and gentle activity, Warmth and warm compresses, Nourishing soups and stews, Gentle movement
patterns.why_this_happens: Qi is the body’s vital force that moves blood through the vessels. Prolonged diabetes drains Qi, leaving it too weak to keep blood flowing smoothly. Blood then stagnates in the tiny channels that nourish the nerves, producing the numbness, tingling, and sharp stabbing pains typical of diabetic neuropathy, especially when the body is at rest and circulation naturally slows.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: pale-dark or pale-purple body with stasis spots, teeth marks, thin white coat. Pulse: deep (沉 chén), weak (弱 ruò), and choppy (涩 sè).
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Qi deficiency means the body’s vital force is too weak to push blood through the vessels, so overexertion and stress drain it further, while rest and gentle movement help conserve and move Qi. Cold constricts the channels and worsens stagnation, whereas warmth dilates them and encourages flow. Nourishing foods build Qi and blood, providing the raw materials for repair, while greasy, sugary foods create dampness and phlegm that further obstruct the channels.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Prioritize gentle daily movement like walking or tai chi to keep blood flowing without draining Qi. Eat warm, nourishing foods such as congee, soups, and stews with dark leafy greens and lean proteins; avoid cold, raw, and sugary foods that weaken digestion and create dampness.

patterns.why_this_happens: Chronic high blood sugar depletes the body's Yin fluids, leaving the nerves and sinews undernourished and dry. This lack of lubrication leads to numbness and tingling, while the resulting empty heat rises and causes burning sensations in the limbs. The dryness also thickens the blood, contributing to stasis and sharp, stabbing pain that worsens at night when Yin should be most abundant.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: red, thin body with cracks, little or no coating, dry surface. Pulse: fine (thin) and rapid, may feel floating and empty at the third position.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Yin is the body's cooling and moistening force. Heat, dryness, and overwork consume Yin, making burning pain and numbness worse. Rest, cooling, and moistening foods help preserve Yin and calm the empty heat that fuels nighttime discomfort.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Avoid spicy, fried, and drying foods that consume Yin. Eat moistening foods like pear, lily bulb, black sesame, and tofu. Sip warm water throughout the day and avoid alcohol and coffee. Prioritize rest and go to bed early to preserve Yin, and practice gentle movement like Tai Chi or restorative yoga rather than intense exercise.

patterns.pattern_name: Cold invading the Channels joints and muscles
patterns.symptoms: ["Sharp, fixed pain in limbs", "Pain worsens with cold, improves with warmth", "Limbs feel cold to the touch", "Numbness in hands and feet", "Stiffness and limited range of motion"]
patterns.worse_with: Cold exposure, Cold raw foods and drinks, Damp, chilly weather, Prolonged inactivity
patterns.better_with: Warmth and warm compresses, Gentle movement, Warm, cooked meals, Moxibustion
patterns.why_this_happens: In diabetic neuropathy, years of high blood sugar deplete Qi and Yang, leaving the body vulnerable to cold. When cold invades, it contracts the channels and congeals blood, much like ice freezing a stream. This obstruction blocks nourishment to the nerves, producing sharp, fixed pain and numbness in the limbs. Because the blockage is cold in nature, symptoms flare in cold environments and ease with warmth.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: pale body, thin white moist coat. Pulse: tight (Jin), deep, and often wiry or choppy.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Cold contracts and freezes the flow of Qi and blood, directly intensifying the channel obstruction that causes pain and numbness. Warmth does the opposite - it relaxes the channels, thaws the stagnation, and restores circulation. Gentle movement encourages blood flow without straining already depleted energy, while moxibustion and warm foods add heat to the body's core, driving out cold from deep within.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Keep limbs warm with layers and avoid cold drafts. Eat warm, cooked foods like soups and stews, adding gentle spices such as ginger and cinnamon. Gentle daily movement like walking helps keep Qi and blood moving, but avoid overexertion. Applying a warm compress or moxibustion to the lower back and painful areas can provide significant relief.

patterns.symptoms: ["Heavy numbness or 'cotton-walking' sensation in the feet", "Sticky taste in the mouth and chest tightness", "Overweight body type", "Fixed, deep stabbing pain that feels heavy", "Thick, white, greasy tongue coating"]
patterns.worse_with: Greasy, fried, or sugary foods, Damp, humid environments, Prolonged inactivity, Overeating or late-night snacking
patterns.better_with: Warm, cooked meals, Gentle movement, Dry, warm weather
patterns.why_this_happens: Chronic diabetes gradually weakens the Spleen, which is responsible for transforming fluids. When the Spleen slows down, fluids accumulate into a sticky, turbid substance called Phlegm-Dampness. This Phlegm settles into the Channels and collaterals, creating a heavy, obstructive blockage that prevents Qi and Blood from reaching the limbs. The result is the characteristic deep numbness and a sensation of walking on cotton, often accompanied by fixed stabbing pain if Blood Stasis also sets in.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: purple or dark body, often swollen with teeth marks, and a white thick greasy coating; sublingual veins distended. Pulse: deep (Chen), and either slippery (Hua) if Phlegm dominates or choppy (Se) if Stasis is more pronounced.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Phlegm is a thick, turbid byproduct of poor digestion. Heavy, greasy foods overwhelm the Spleen, turning nourishment into Dampness and Phlegm that clogs the channels-hence the worsening of numbness. Damp weather seeps into the body and congeals, while a sedentary lifestyle allows Qi to stagnate, giving Phlegm a chance to settle. On the other hand, light, warm foods are easy to transform, and movement acts like a bellows, fanning Qi and Blood through the collaterals to sweep Phlegm away.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Keep meals light and warm, favoring cooked vegetables, Job's tears (Yi Yi Ren), and radish, which help drain Dampness. Strictly avoid greasy, fried, dairy-rich, and sugary foods, as they directly generate Phlegm. Gentle daily movement like walking or tai chi is essential to keep Qi and fluids circulating; long periods of sitting still allow Phlegm to settle deeper into the channels.

faqs.question: Can acupuncture really help with numbness from diabetes?
faqs.answer: Yes. Acupuncture can improve blood flow to the nerves and reduce pain signals. Many patients report less tingling and burning after several sessions. The effect is gradual and works best when combined with herbal medicine to address the underlying pattern.

faqs.question: How long does it take to feel relief?
faqs.answer: Some people notice a reduction in pain within 2-3 weeks, but numbness often takes longer - typically 6-12 weeks of consistent treatment. Because nerve tissue heals slowly, patience and regular sessions are essential.

faqs.question: Can I take herbs with my diabetes medications?
faqs.answer: Yes, but you must monitor your blood sugar closely. Some herbs can lower blood glucose, so your medication dosage may need adjustment. Always inform both your TCM practitioner and your prescribing doctor about all treatments you are using. Never stop or change your diabetes medication without medical supervision.

faqs.question: Is it safe if I have open sores or ulcers?
faqs.answer: Acupuncture should not be performed directly on open wounds or infected areas. However, your practitioner can use distal points on other parts of the body to treat the neuropathy without touching the ulcer. Herbal medicine can also be taken orally. Always let your practitioner know about any skin breaks before treatment. For signs of infection, seek immediate medical care.

faqs.question: Will the treatment cure my neuropathy?
faqs.answer: TCM cannot reverse dead nerve tissue, but it can often halt progression, reduce pain and numbness, and improve quality of life. The goal is to restore function and prevent further damage by addressing the underlying deficiency and obstruction. Many patients achieve significant, lasting relief.

faqs.question: Do I need to change my diet?
faqs.answer: Yes. Diet is crucial in TCM for diabetes and neuropathy. You'll generally be advised to avoid sugar, refined carbohydrates, and cold, raw foods that weaken the Spleen. Instead, eat warming, cooked meals and foods that nourish Qi and blood, such as dark leafy greens, beets, lean meats, and whole grains.

research.title: Acupuncture for diabetic peripheral neuropathy: a systematic review and meta-analysis
research.description: This meta-analysis pooled data from 25 RCTs involving over 1,600 patients. Acupuncture significantly improved total effective rate, pain scores, and nerve conduction velocity compared to conventional medications. Subgroup analysis suggested that electroacupuncture and manual acupuncture were both effective, with a low incidence of adverse events.
research.periodical: Chen W, Yang GY, Liu B, Manheimer E, Liu JP. Acupuncture for diabetic peripheral neuropathy: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Evidence-Based Complementary and Alternative Medicine. 2013;2013:543673.

research.title: Chinese herbal medicine for diabetic peripheral neuropathy
research.description: This Cochrane systematic review assessed 39 RCTs comparing Chinese herbal medicine to placebo, conventional drugs, or other interventions. Some herbal formulas, especially those containing blood-invigorating and Qi-tonifying herbs, showed significant improvement in global symptom scores and nerve conduction. The review highlighted the need for larger, better-designed trials.
research.periodical: Liu JP, Zhang M, Wang W, Grimsgaard S. Chinese herbal medicine for diabetic peripheral neuropathy. Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. 2013, Issue 2. Art. No.: CD007796.

research.title: Acupuncture for the treatment of chronic painful peripheral diabetic neuropathy: a long-term study
research.description: In this prospective study, 46 patients with chronic painful diabetic neuropathy received a course of 10 acupuncture sessions. Significant improvements in pain scores were observed in 34 patients (74%), with benefits maintained for up to 6 months after treatment. No serious adverse effects were reported.
research.periodical: Abuaisha BB, Costanzi JB, Boulton AJ. Acupuncture for the treatment of chronic painful peripheral diabetic neuropathy: a long-term study. Diabetes Research and Clinical Practice. 1998;39(2):115-121.
